Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Judean presence at Lod is the list of returnees from the Babylonian exile; no documented Judahite presence before 586 BCE was found (Lod reportedly lay outside Iron Age Benjamin; settlement of Benjaminites spread west to Lod, Hadid and Ono in the Persian period per Tavger 2022, not accessed). Ezra 2:33: 'Of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty-five.' Return list traditionally dated to the return under Cyrus, c. 538 BCE (the list may be composite of several returns). The figure 725 covers three towns combined and counts returnees, not Lod's resident population, so Population is blank.

Nehemiah 7:37: 'Of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, seven hundred twenty-one' - the same returnee list as Ezra 2 repeated in Nehemiah with a different figure (721 vs 725). Combined figure for three towns; Population blank. Year c. 445 BCE (Nehemiah's governorship), approximate.

Nehemiah 11:31-35: 'The people of Benjamin also lived ... Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat, Lod, and Ono, the valley of artisans.' Literary attestation of Judean (Benjaminite) residents at Lod in Nehemiah's time; c. 445-432 BCE, approximate. No count.

Israeli Institute of Archaeology history of Lod (no author named): 'Lod became an important Jewish center during the Persian period.' Persian period 539-332 BCE, midpoint -435. No figure for this period.

Raviv 2019 (Tel Aviv 46/2, abstract only): new archaeological evidence and re-examination of surveys indicate that Jews were already the majority of the population in the toparchies of Ephraim, Ramathaim and Lod before the Hasmonean Revolt. Regional (toparchy-level) statement, not a town count. Year c. early 2nd c. BCE before 167 BCE, approximate.

1 Maccabees 11:34: Demetrius II confirms to Jonathan the borders of Judea and 'the three governments of Aphaerema and Lydda and Ramathaim', added to Judea from Samaria, for all who sacrifice in Jerusalem. Annexation of Lod district to Hasmonean Judea, c. 145 BCE (Demetrius II's accession; an earlier offer by Demetrius I, 1 Macc 10:30, 38, c. 152 BCE). Event; no count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (M. Avi-Yonah) via JVL: Lod 'was detached from Samaria and given to Jonathan the Hasmonean by Demetrius II in 145 B.C.E.', became a toparchy of Judea, and 'In Maccabean times it was a purely Jewish town.' Characterization of the whole town as Jewish; date given only as Maccabean/Hasmonean times, Hasmonean period 140-37 BCE midpoint -90. No count.

Israeli Institute of Archaeology history of Lod (no author or method given): after Demetrius proposed moving Lod to Judea 'due to its Jewish majority' and the Seleucids transferred it to the Hasmoneans as capital of a Judean district, the settlement moved south (area of St George Church/al-Omri Mosque) and 'During this period Lod grew larger and more important, with a population of about 2,500.' Total population of a town the same source describes as Jewish-majority (rural area also Jewish-majority); dated only to the Hellenistic/Hasmonean period, Hasmonean period 140-37 BCE midpoint -90.

Etya 2024 (Lod journal vol. 10, Table 1): Lod (Neve Yaraq) Stratum 7, isolated structures and installations, no destruction layer, attributed by the excavators (Rosenberger and Shavit 1994) to the days of Alexander Jannaeus (with a question mark); footnote notes Hellenistic remains in other parts of Lod. Etya concludes that material culture of Hasmonean affiliation appears clearly in Lod valley sites only in the late 2nd-early 1st c. BCE. Settlement evidence at Lod in the Hasmonean period; no explicit Jewish markers reported for this Lod stratum. Jannaeus 103-76 BCE, c. -90.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.208 (decree of Julius Caesar for Hyrcanus II and the Jews): 'and let them enjoy the like privileges in Lydda.' Confirms Jewish (Hasmonean/high-priestly) rights at Lydda. Caesar's decrees 47-44 BCE; c. -47.

Encyclopaedia Judaica via JVL: 'In 43 B.C.E. its inhabitants were sold into slavery by Cassius, the governor of Syria' (Josephus, Ant. 14.275 lists Gophna, Emmaus, Lydda and Thamna as the four towns enslaved for failing to pay tribute). Enslavement of the Jewish townspeople; they were freed c. 41 BCE, so not a documented permanent absence; Population blank. No count.

Wikipedia (last resort; cites Josephus War 1.11.2 and Ant. 14.12.2-5): 'In 43 BC, Cassius ... sold the inhabitants of Lod into slavery, but they were set free two years later by Mark Antony.' Event: liberation and return of the enslaved inhabitants, c. 41 BCE.

Mishnah Maaser Sheni 5:2 (describing Temple-era practice): fourth-year vineyard produce was brought up to Jerusalem from a day's journey in each direction, bounded by 'Eilat to the south, Akrabat on the north, Lod to the west, and the Jordan to the east.' Indirect evidence of Lod as the western edge of the Judean agricultural hinterland of Jerusalem before 70 CE; no count. Date only 'Temple times'; early Roman midpoint 4 CE, approximate.

Acts 9:32-38: Peter 'came down also to the saints living in Lydda', healed Aeneas, bedridden eight years; 'all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.' Attests a group of Jesus-following Jews at Lydda (a subset of the Jewish community); the 'all residents' phrase is rhetorical. c. 35-40 CE, approximate.

Hadashot Arkheologiyot 128 (2016), 'Lod, the Lod Mosaic' (Gorzalczany et al.), Newe Yaraq neighbourhood: Stratum VIII, Early Roman building (1st-2nd c. CE) with mosaic floor; fragments of stone cups in adjacent accumulations are taken as 'evidence of a Jewish community that resided at the site'; 'The inhabitants of the ancient building were probably Jewish.' Archaeological presence of Jewish residents; dating spans 1st-2nd c. CE (earliest phase 1st c. CE), so c. 50 CE with possible post-70 use.

Josephus, War 2.242-244: the Syrian governor Ummidius Quadratus came to Lydda, heard the Samaritan-Jewish dispute and beheaded eighteen Jews 'concerned in that fight', then went up from Lydda to Jerusalem. The 18 are executed participants in the clash, not necessarily residents; number kept out of Population. c. 51-52 CE (procuratorship of Cumanus).

Josephus, Antiquities 20.130: Quadratus 'came to a certain village called Lydda, which was not less than a city in largeness.' Indicates a large Jewish settlement with village legal status, c. 51-52 CE; no count.

Josephus, War 2.515-516: when Cestius Gallus marched from Antipatris to Lydda 'he found the city empty of its men, for the whole multitude were gone up to Jerusalem to the feast of tabernacles'; he killed fifty who showed themselves and burned the city. Shows a Jewish population observing the pilgrimage festival; the 50 killed is a casualty count (Notes only). Town burned, autumn 66 CE; not a documented abandonment.

Josephus, War 2.567: in the rebel appointment of commanders, 'Lydda was also added to his portion, and Joppa, and Emmaus' (John the Essene, in charge of the toparchy of Thamna). Lydda under the Jewish revolutionary administration, late 66 CE.
Josephus, War 3.55: Lydda listed among the toparchies of Judea ('Thamna, and Lydda, and Emmaus ...'), i.e. district capital of a Jewish toparchy at the time of Vespasian's campaign, c. 67 CE.

Josephus, War 4.444: Vespasian 'passed on to Lydda and Jamnia; and when both these cities had come over to him, he placed a great many of those that had come over to him [from other places] as inhabitants therein.' Surrender of the town and settlement of surrendered Jews there, spring 68 CE; no count.

Rosenfeld 2024 (Lod, Lydda, Diospolis vol. 2): Lod was seat of the toparchy of the Plain of Lod from the Hasmonean period to 70 CE; after 68 most residents stayed, with surrendered people added. He estimates Lod's total population for 70-132 CE at about 4,100-6,000 (25 persons per dunam over c. 130-220 dunams, or up to c. 400 dunams after Ashkenazi et al. 2016), noting that non-Jews also lived there after the town expanded. Total population of a mixed town, dated mostly after the period; Population blank.
